title: The oddest member of the Leo Triplet
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3628 in the Leo Triplet, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 3628 · constellation Leo · about 35 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 3628 is seen perfectly edge-on, the way we see the Milky Way on a clear night, so its spiral arms are hidden. A dark band of dust runs along its disc and is visibly warped outwards by gravitational tugs from its neighbours. The central bulge is boxy, or peanut-shaped, and appears as a faint X.

The galaxy lies about 35 million light-years away towards Leo and belongs to the Leo Triplet with Messier 65 and Messier 66, which are not in this picture. Charles Messier found those two in 1780, but NGC 3628 is fainter and slipped past his small telescope. William Herschel catalogued it four years later.

The deep image reveals many galaxies of different shapes and colours. A fuzzy blob at the centre is a diffuse satellite galaxy, and fuzzy reddish spots in the halo are globular clusters. Two blue, star-like points near the lower edge are quasars, energetic galaxies billions of light-years away.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.84 x 5.27 arcminutes) and distance (35 million light years), the frame spans roughly 70,000 × 54,000 light-years. Its light set out about 35 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope observed NGC 3628 in visible light through B, V and R filters, for a total of just under an hour. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The nearly hour-long exposure collects far more light than the eye, bringing out faint globular clusters, background galaxies and quasars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Because of its odd shape, NGC 3628 appears as Arp 317 in a 1966 catalogue, the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies. The image comes from FORS2 on the VLT, combining B, V and R exposures totalling just under an hour. The field is about 7 arcminutes across, too narrow to fit the whole galaxy.
alt: An edge-on galaxy with a warped dark dust lane, surrounded by small background galaxies, reddish spots and two blue points near the bottom.
